posts.note: Guest essay by clinical trial participant Jonathan Rosenberg; body text is his, not the author's. Only the author's outro promise of a follow-up installment is logged. Jonathan's own retrospective predictions about his illness were not logged (not the author's claims).
Travel essay on Kyoto culture. Remark that The Line (Saudi linear city) is 'not a great way to organize a city' is a design opinion with no future state and was not logged.
Annals of Internal Medicine antidepressant weight-gain study review plus a case for brain stimulation as first-line treatment. Many 'should/need to' sentences are normative and were not logged.
Science-communication essay from the Brain Stimulation meeting in Kobe. One generic conditional about training as explainers logged as borderline.
Announcement of a Bipolar Disorders paper with Alex Mendelsohn and Awais Aftab on standardized lithium levels. No forward-looking claims.
Recycled column (Neurowrap vs Magnus Medical scam-detection) with a new intro about UnitedHealth Group. The body and its upcoming-topics list and Nobel footnote date from the original publication.

Review of a Dutch cost-effectiveness study of medication vs no medication in childhood ADHD/ODD. Personal remark that the author's daughter 'probably has ADHD' is about a family member's health, not a state of the world, and was not logged. Closing 'we need better treatments' is normative.
Podcast appearance announcement (Mind The Force). No forward-looking claims.
Review of JAMA Health Forum paper on physician turnover after private equity exits. Study-finding generalizations logged only where phrased as standing expectations.

statements.quote: Jonathan’s story ends well, I promise. ... He has more to say, stay tuned!
statements.context: Author's outro after guest Jonathan Rosenberg's first-person account of depression (he enrolled in an accelerated TMS study). The author promises the story will be continued in a later installment and that it ends well.
statements.note: Own-newsletter content promise; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: But at this meeting, a bunch of scientist, many of whom are also practicing physicians, will be sharing data around the role of non-medication treatments for brain disorders.
statements.context: Author is in Kobe, Japan to present data at the Brain Stimulation conference. He states that at this meeting scientists will share data on non-medication (brain stimulation) treatments for brain disorders, mainly depression.
statements.note: Near-term event statement about a conference the author is attending; low forecast value.

statements.quote: Psychiatry could be a discipline in which people come to a doctor for help with their problems, and the doctor prescribes a treatment. And that treatment? Wait for it. It might not be a pill. It might be something else entirely. It might be a treatment that stimulates the brain, and relieves the depression, and does not include a daily oral medication that causes risk of weight gain, movement disorders, emotional blunting, sexual side effects, and a range of other problems.
statements.context: Setup to the Annals of Internal Medicine antidepressant weight-gain study. The author sketches a possible future for psychiatry in which brain stimulation, not a daily pill, is the prescribed treatment for depression.
statements.note: Vision statement with hedges; borderline between forecast and advocacy. Author has a commercial stake in brain stimulation clinics.

statements.quote: We could use brain stimulation as a first line treatment, we could do research about brain stimulation as a first line treatment, we'd have to pay for it though.
statements.context: Same setup: the author argues brain stimulation could become a first-line depression treatment and could be researched as such, conditional on payment for it.
statements.note: Possibility claim with a payment condition; borderline advocacy. Related to the preceding vision statement.

statements.quote: The harder we train as explainers, and story tellers, the better we might be at getting the understanding of our work to the world.
statements.context: Author's challenge to academic journals and scientists to require a funny video or meme alongside each paper (citing NEJM partnering with Dr. Glaucomflecken). Conditional expectation that training in storytelling improves public understanding of science.
statements.note: Generic conditional with no specific resolvable state; borderline. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: I’m going to be on a plane flying back from Japan today, so this recycled column will be a hit with the several thousand people who read this now who didn’t read the newsletter back when this was published.
statements.context: New intro to a recycled scam-detection column. The author predicts the repost will be a hit with newer subscribers.
statements.note: Light, self-referential prediction about own newsletter reception. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: So my guess is that Neurowrap is probably a scam.
statements.context: Conclusion of the website-only scam-detection walkthrough comparing the direct-to-consumer 'Neurowrap' device (claims FDA approval 'or' clearance, 'happy hormones', naturopath spokesman) with Magnus Medical (FDA clearance language, hiring, waitlist). The author judges Neurowrap is probably a scam and Magnus Medical is not.
statements.note: Present-state judgment about a product's legitimacy, not a future state; logged for recall. From the recycled original column.

statements.quote: Make sure to subscribe now to not miss out on a single—doubtless breathtaking—upcoming topic: ... The true story of why I use my middle name online
statements.context: Closing of the recycled column: list of upcoming newsletter topics - private equity in teen paranormal romance (joke), major healthcare entities' statements, due diligence on Silicon Valley failures, personal stories of hope, guides to negotiating IP and arbitration agreements, and why the author uses his middle name online.
statements.note: Own-newsletter content plan, partly joking; recycled from the original publication date. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: With this footnote, I will continue my ongoing campaign to urge the Nobel committee to select Nolan Williams, MD, for the 2023 Nobel prize in medicine and physiology, for his research around the technology commercialized by Magnus Medical.
statements.context: Footnote to the recycled column. The author restates his campaign for Nolan Williams (Stanford, SAINT/Magnus Medical technology) to receive the 2023 Nobel Prize in medicine.
statements.note: Wish/advocacy, not a prediction; the 2023 date is already past at repost (2025-02-25). Logged for recall with normative flag.

statements.quote: After a private equity acquisition of a practice, doctors are highly likely to leave that practice in the next two years, as measured by billing out of another practice.
statements.context: Summary of the JAMA Health Forum case-control study 'Sale of Private Equity-Owned Physician Practices and Physician Turnover'. The author states as a standing rule that physicians are highly likely to leave a practice within two years of a PE acquisition/exit (roughly 20 percent more likely to work elsewhere).
statements.note: Generalization of a study finding phrased as a standing expectation; borderline past analysis. Coder may reclassify.

statements.quote: In fact, it's likely that a lot of these private equity roll ups end up becoming part of Optum.
statements.context: After noting that physicians who leave PE-exited practices go to work for large groups such as hospitals or UnitedHealth (Optum employs about 10 percent of US physicians), the author predicts many PE physician-practice roll-ups will end up as part of Optum.

statements.quote: United is like the Apex predator of private equity acquisitions. They're getting bought by PE to either be bankrupted, or acquired by a company like Optum.
statements.context: Closing of the PE physician-turnover post. The author claims physician practices bought by private equity end up either bankrupt or acquired by a company like Optum (UnitedHealth Group).
statements.note: Restates the preceding Optum call as a binary fate for PE-acquired practices; compound claim.
